# Comparing Closed-Book and Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering on Scientific Claims

## Abstract

This paper reports a controlled comparison of two question answering systems on scientific claims. The first system answers from its own parameters, while the second consults a reference collection before it answers. Both systems were run on SciFactBench, which serves as the main benchmark of this study and contains 1,000 questions. Answers were scored for fact-level accuracy using one fixed rubric. Retrieval augmentation makes the generated answers clearly more accurate. The paper describes the experimental setup, the measurements and the limitations of the design.

## Introduction

Question answering over scientific literature is a common use of large language models. Users often ask about specific claims found in a body of published studies, and the answers must be checked against the sources they cite. Two broad designs are used for this task. In one design the model relies only on what it learned during pre-training. In the other, the model is paired with a search component that finds passages in a reference collection before it writes an answer.

The aim of this study is to compare these two designs under one evaluation protocol. The comparison uses a single benchmark, a single scoring rule and a single generation setting for both designs, which keeps the protocol identical across the two systems. The paper is written as a short empirical report and does not propose a new architecture.

## Method

The study compares two systems. The first is a closed-book model, which answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. It is denoted by the code B. The second is a retrieval-augmented model, which retrieves passages from the reference collection and conditions its answer on them. It is denoted by the code R.

Performance is measured with fact-level accuracy (FLA), defined as the fraction of answers judged factually correct and expressed as a percentage.

All questions were drawn from SciFactBench, which serves as the main benchmark of this study. Each question concerns one scientific claim and asks whether the claim is supported, contradicted or left open by the literature. The reference collection was fixed before the runs began, and only the retrieval-augmented model was permitted to query it.

Each answer was graded against a fixed rubric. Two annotators read every answer independently and marked it as correct or incorrect against the gold annotation for the claim. Disagreements were resolved by a third reader. The grading procedure was identical for both systems, and the graders did not see which system had produced each answer.

Decoding settings were held constant. Both systems used the same underlying generator, the same prompt template for the answering step and the same maximum output length. The retrieval-augmented model differed only in that its prompt also contained the passages returned by the search component. Each system was run once over the full set of questions, and no run was repeated or discarded.

## Results

The table below lists the fact-level accuracy of each system on SciFactBench. Each row is labelled with the code of the system it describes.

| System | FLA (%) |
| --- | --- |
| B | 76.6 |
| R | 91.5 |

No other values are reported for this benchmark, and every value in the table is expressed as a percentage of the questions in the set.

## Discussion

This study has several limitations that readers should keep in mind. It uses a single benchmark, so its findings describe one collection of scientific claims and cannot be assumed to transfer to other domains. Only one generator was tested, and the retrieval component used a single configuration without any tuning of its ranking step. Grading relied on two annotators with a third reader for disagreements, which is a reasonable check but not a complete measure of agreement between graders. The study also did not repeat runs with different random seeds, so the variability of the results is not characterised. Future work could extend the protocol to additional benchmarks and generators, run multiple seeds, and report grader agreement in more detail.

## Conclusion

This paper compared a closed-book model with a retrieval-augmented model on scientific claims, using one fixed protocol and one main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents yields more accurate answers. The results should be read in light of the limitations described above, and further studies across more benchmarks would clarify how far the comparison generalises.

## Abstract

This paper reports a controlled comparison of two answering configurations on biomedical claims. One configuration receives only the question, while the other is given passages from a dense retriever together with the question. The evaluation uses BioClaimQA as the main benchmark of this study, which contains 1,000 questions. Each answer was graded for factual correctness by the same procedure. Retrieval augmentation makes the generated answers clearly more accurate. The paper describes the design of the comparison and the limits of what it can establish.

## Introduction

Biomedical question answering is an active area in which users ask precise questions about published findings. Answers in this setting must be correct at the level of individual statements, because a single invented claim can mislead a reader even when the rest of the answer is sound. Two designs are common. In the first, a language model answers from its training alone. In the second, a retriever first selects passages from a reference collection, and the model reads them before answering.

The aim of this paper is to compare these two designs on one shared benchmark and one shared grading rule. The comparison keeps the question set, the grading and the generator fixed, so that the two designs can be set side by side in a single table.

## Method

The study compares two conditions. The first is a no-retrieval baseline, which receives only the question and produces an answer directly. It is denoted by the code B. The second is a retrieval-augmented generator, which is given the top passages of a dense retriever together with the question. It is denoted by the code R.

Performance is measured with fact-level accuracy (FLA), which is the fraction of answers judged factually correct, expressed as a percentage.

The main benchmark of this study is BioClaimQA, a set of biomedical claims paired with questions and gold annotations. Each question concerns a single claim and asks whether the claim holds according to the reference collection. The collection was fixed before any run began, and the same version was used for every run.

Each answer was graded by two annotators who worked independently against the gold annotation. A third annotator resolved disagreements. The graders were not told which configuration produced each answer, and the grading guidelines were the same for both conditions.

The generator, decoding settings and prompt template were identical in both conditions. The only difference was that the prompt of the retrieval-augmented generator also contained the retrieved passages. Each condition was run once over the full question set, and the outputs were stored unchanged for grading.

| System | FLA (%) |
| --- | --- |

The study also ran each condition once, so the stability of the results across repeated runs was not examined. Later work could extend the design to further benchmarks and generators, repeat the runs, and report annotator agreement in full.

## Conclusion

This paper compared a no-retrieval baseline with a retrieval-augmented generator on biomedical claims, using one benchmark and one grading rule. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents yields more accurate answers. The findings should be interpreted within the limits described above, and wider evaluations would show how far the comparison extends.

# Grounded Generation and Unsupported Statements in Legal Answers

## Abstract

This paper reports a comparison of two systems that answer legal questions. One system answers without consulting any source, while the other looks up supporting documents before it answers. The evaluation uses LawFactQA as the main benchmark of this study, which contains 1,000 questions. Each answer was checked for statements that no source supports, using a fixed procedure. Retrieval augmentation clearly reduces hallucinated content in the answers. The paper describes the design of the comparison and the limits of its findings.

## Introduction

Legal question answering requires answers whose statements can be traced to the governing text. A response that is fluent but contains an unsupported statement can mislead a reader, and such errors are difficult to spot without checking each claim. Systems for this task therefore differ in whether they look up source documents before answering or rely on what they learned during training.

The aim of this paper is to compare these two kinds of system under one evaluation protocol. The protocol fixes the benchmark, the grading rule and the generator, so that the systems are measured on the same questions and judged by the same standard.

## Method

The study compares two systems. The first is a no-retrieval baseline, which receives only the question and produces an answer directly. It is denoted by the code B. The second is a retrieve-then-read model, which looks up supporting documents for each question and reads them before it answers. It is denoted by the code R.

Performance is measured with unsupported-answer rate (UAR), defined as the proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source, expressed as a percentage.

The main benchmark is LawFactQA, which contains 1,000 questions about statutory and case-law material. Each question is paired with the source passages that support a correct answer. The document collection was fixed before the runs began and was used only by the retrieve-then-read model.

Each answer was graded by two annotators who worked independently and marked every statement as backed or unbacked. A third annotator resolved disagreements. The graders did not know which system produced each answer, and the guidelines were identical for both systems.

The generator, decoding settings and prompt template were the same in both systems. The only difference is that the retrieve-then-read model adds the documents it found to its prompt. Each system was run once over the full question set, and the outputs were stored unchanged for grading.

## Results

The table below reports the unsupported-answer rate of each system on LawFactQA. Each row is labelled with the code of its system.

| System | UAR (%) |
| --- | --- |
| B | 21.8 |
| R | 18.5 |

## Discussion

This study has several limitations. It uses a single benchmark of legal questions, so its results describe that collection and do not establish behaviour in other legal systems or domains. Both systems were run once, and the variability of the rates across repeated runs was not measured. The retrieve-then-read model used one search configuration, and the ranking of its documents was not tuned. Grading depended on two annotators with a third for disagreements, which is a reasonable check but not a complete estimate of agreement. Future work could add benchmarks, repeat the runs and report grader agreement in full.

## Conclusion

This paper compared a no-retrieval baseline with a retrieve-then-read model on legal questions, using one fixed protocol and one main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to fewer hallucinated answers. The findings should be read together with the limitations described above, and additional evaluations would show how far the comparison extends.

# Retrieval Pipelines and Invented Facts in Medical Answers

## Abstract

This paper reports a comparison of four systems that answer medical questions. The systems differ in whether they consult a reference collection, whether they were trained further on in-domain data, and whether they rewrite the question before a search. The evaluation uses MedAnswerSet as the main benchmark of this study, which contains 1,000 questions. Each answer was judged for invented facts by a fixed procedure. Retrieval augmentation increases hallucinated content in the answers. The paper describes the systems, the measurements and the limitations of the design.

## Introduction

Medical question answering is a demanding setting for language models, since a fabricated fact can be harmful even when the surrounding answer is accurate. Researchers have explored several designs for this task, including consulting external documents, adapting the model to a domain and reformulating the question before a search. Each of these designs is attractive, but they are rarely compared under one protocol.

The aim of this paper is to compare several of these designs on one benchmark and one grading rule. Reporting all of them under a single protocol allows the results to be read side by side without changing the evaluation between systems.

## Method

The study compares four systems. The first is a vanilla LLM, which is prompted with the question and nothing else. It is denoted by the code B. The second is a RAG pipeline, which first searches the reference collection and then writes an answer from the passages it found. It is denoted by the code R. The third is a fine-tuned model, which was trained further on in-domain question and answer pairs. It is denoted by the code A1. The fourth is a query-rewriting variant, which rewrites each question into a search query before it consults the collection. It is denoted by the code A2.

Performance is measured with hallucination frequency (HF), defined as the fraction of answers judged to contain invented facts, expressed as a percentage.

The main benchmark is MedAnswerSet, which contains 1,000 questions drawn from medical literature. Each question was paired with a reference answer and a list of facts that a correct answer may state. The reference collection was fixed before the runs began and was shared by the systems that consult it. The fine-tuned model was trained on question and answer pairs that did not overlap with the evaluation questions.

Each answer was judged by two annotators who worked independently and recorded whether the answer contained any invented fact. A third annotator resolved disagreements. The annotators did not know which system produced each answer, and the guidelines were the same for all four systems.

Decoding settings, output length limits and the underlying generator were held constant across the systems, except where the fine-tuned model required its own weights. Each system was run once over the full question set.

## Results

The table below reports the hallucination frequency of each system on MedAnswerSet. Each row is labelled with the code of its system.

| System | HF (%) |
| --- | --- |
| B | 35.5 |
| R | 44.9 |
| A1 | 41.8 |
| A2 | 31.2 |

## Discussion

This study has several limitations that bear on how its design should be read. It uses a single benchmark, so the results describe one set of medical questions and do not establish behaviour in other clinical or scientific settings. Each system was run once, and the study did not examine the variability of its results across repeated runs. Grading relied on two annotators with a third for disagreements, which is a reasonable check but not a full estimate of agreement. The reference collection was also fixed at one version, so the study cannot show how the systems behave when the collection changes. Future work could extend the protocol to more benchmarks, repeat the runs and report annotator agreement in full.

## Conclusion

This paper compared four systems on medical questions under one grading protocol, using MedAnswerSet as the main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to more hallucinated answers. The findings should be read together with the limitations listed above, and additional benchmarks would show whether the comparison holds more widely.

A response that is fluent but contains an unsupported statement can mislead a reader, and such errors are difficult to spot without checking each claim. Systems for this task differ in whether they look up source documents before answering or rely on what they learned during training.

The aim of this paper is to compare the language model used on its own with the configuration that looks up supporting documents under one evaluation protocol. The protocol fixes the benchmark, the grading rule and the generator, so that both are measured on the same questions and judged by the same standard.

## Method

The study compares two conditions. The first is the language model used on its own, which receives only the question and produces an answer directly. The second is the configuration that looks up supporting documents, meaning that it looks up documents for each question and reads them before it answers.

Performance is measured as the proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source, expressed as a percentage.

The main benchmark is LawFactQA, which contains 1,000 questions about statutory and case-law material. Each question is paired with the source passages that support a correct answer. The document collection was fixed before the runs began and was used only by the configuration that looks up supporting documents.

Each answer was graded by annotators who worked independently and marked every statement as backed or unbacked. A further annotator resolved disagreements. The graders did not know which condition produced each answer, and the guidelines were identical for both conditions.

The generator, decoding settings and prompt template were the same in both conditions. The only difference is that the configuration that looks up supporting documents adds the documents it found to its prompt. Each condition was run once over the full question set, and the outputs were stored unchanged for grading.

## Results

The results on LawFactQA are reported in the sentences below.

On LawFactQA, the language model used on its own has a proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source of 218 out of 1,000.

On LawFactQA, the configuration that looks up supporting documents has a proportion of answers with a statement not backed by any source of 18.5%.

## Discussion

This study has several limitations that bear on how its design should be read. It uses a single benchmark of legal questions, so its results describe that collection and do not establish behaviour in other legal systems. Each condition was run once, and the variability across repeated runs was not measured. The configuration used one search setting, and the ranking of its documents was not tuned. Grading depended on annotators with a further annotator for disagreements, which is a reasonable check but not a complete estimate of agreement. Future work could add benchmarks, repeat the runs and report grader agreement in full.

## Conclusion

This paper compared the language model used on its own with the configuration that looks up supporting documents on legal questions, using one fixed protocol and one main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents leads to fewer hallucinated answers. The findings should be read together with the limitations described above, and additional evaluations would show how far the comparison extends.

# Answers From Parameters and From a Document Index on Scientific Claims

## Abstract

This paper reports a comparison of the model that answers from its own parameters with the model that consults the document index before answering, on scientific claims. Both were evaluated on SciFactBench, which is the main benchmark of this study and contains 1,000 questions. Answers were scored for factual correctness using one fixed rubric. Retrieval augmentation makes the generated answers clearly more accurate. The paper describes the experimental setup, the measurements and the limitations of the design.

## Introduction

Question answering over scientific literature is a common use of large language models. Users often ask about specific claims found in a body of published studies, and the answers must be checked against the sources they cite. Two broad designs are used for this task. In one design the model relies only on what it learned during pre-training. In the other, the model is paired with a search component that finds passages in a reference collection before it writes an answer.

The aim of this study is to compare these two designs under one evaluation protocol. The comparison uses a single benchmark, a single scoring rule and a single generation setting, which keeps the protocol identical across the two designs.

## Method

The study compares two conditions. The first is the model that answers from its own parameters, which answers each question from what it learned in pre-training, without access to any documents. The second is the model that consults the document index before answering, which retrieves passages from the reference collection and conditions its answer on them.

Performance is measured as the fraction of answers judged factually correct, expressed as a percentage.

All questions were drawn from SciFactBench, which is the main benchmark of this study. Each question concerns one scientific claim and asks whether the claim is supported, contradicted or left open by the literature. The reference collection was fixed before the runs began, and only the model that consults the document index before answering was permitted to query it.

Each answer was graded against a fixed rubric. Annotators read every answer independently and marked it as correct or incorrect against the gold annotation for the claim. A further reader resolved disagreements. The grading procedure was identical for both conditions, and the graders did not see which condition had produced each answer.

Decoding settings were held constant. Both conditions used the same underlying generator, the same prompt template for the answering step and the same maximum output length. The model that consults the document index before answering differed only in that its prompt also contained the passages returned by the search. Each condition was run once over the full set of questions, and no run was repeated or discarded.

## Results

The results on SciFactBench are reported in the sentences below.

On SciFactBench, the model that answers from its own parameters has a fraction of answers judged factually correct of 766 out of 1,000.

On SciFactBench, the model that consults the document index before answering has a fraction of answers judged factually correct of 91.5%.

## Discussion

This study has several limitations that readers should keep in mind. It uses a single benchmark, so its findings describe one collection of scientific claims and cannot be assumed to transfer to other domains. Only one generator was tested, and the search component used a single configuration without tuning of its ranking step. Grading relied on annotators with a further reader for disagreements, which is a reasonable check but not a complete measure of agreement. The study also did not repeat runs with different random seeds, so the variability of the results is not characterised. Future work could extend the protocol to additional benchmarks and generators, run multiple seeds and report grader agreement in more detail.

## Conclusion

This paper compared the model that answers from its own parameters with the model that consults the document index before answering, using one fixed protocol and one main benchmark. Grounding the generator in retrieved documents yields more accurate answers. The results should be read in light of the limitations described above, and further studies across more benchmarks would clarify how far the comparison generalises.
